newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Indonesia wants better monitoring of mining rights.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia wants better monitoring of mining rights.

text.p: Indonesia wants to increase the monitoring of companies applying for mining rights in an attempt to increase the number of projects brought to fruition, a senior Indonesian mining official said on Tuesday.

"Over the past 10 years, we have had about 132 companies apply for mining rights (and) out of those only about 42 (companies) are left," said Rozik. B. Soetjipto, director of mining industry development under Indonesia's Directorate General of Mines.
The companies were granted plots on parliamentary approval, but many held them for a short time before selling them at a profit to other companies, he said.
"We want serious companies to apply and we would like to increase the monitoring so the success rate improves," he said.
He was speaking at an Asian Gold Congress in Hong Kong.
New regulations would ensure Indonesia attracted mining companies with the expertise and resources for exploration and mineral development, he added.
Indonesia would also speed up administrative procedures for contract and mining right applications, and boost supervision during implementation, Soetjipto said.

The discovery by Canadian firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd of huge gold deposits in Busang, in eastern Kalimantan, had resulted in a rush of interest from foreign exploration companies, particularly from Canada, Soetjipto said.

By June 1996, 42 foreign companies had mining Contracts of Work (COWs) in Indonesia for production, commissioning, conducting feasibilty studies and exploration. Of those, 13 were conducting feasibility studies on Kalimantan island.
The discovery of gold in Busang last year caused an explosion of interest in gold and base metal exploration which could significantly increase gold production in the early 21st Century, he said.
Indonesia was known to have more than 2,650 tonnes of gold calculated from its past and present resources, he said.
Indonesia is ranked third after China and India in mineral potential, according to an ANZ McCaughan's Company Perceptions survey in 1994.
